newsitem.title: THAILAND: Wrangling begins over Thailand's top job.
newsitem.headline: Wrangling begins over Thailand's top job.

text.p: Wrangling began in earnest as key members of Thailand's six-party coalition government met on Sunday to negotiate over who would become the new prime minister after Banharn Silpa-archa's resignation.

"For the next six days, political negotiations will be very intense," Somjai Phagaphasvivat, political scientist at Thammasat University, told Reuters. "The coalition partners are manoeuvring against time."
Banharn, who said on Saturday he would step down in seven days after finding a suitable replacement, did not plan to join the Sunday meeting, an official from his Chart Thai party said.
Instead Banharn, who announced his resignation after a bruising no-confidence debate against him in parliament last week, would go to his home province of Suphan Buri to rest.

Political analysts and politicians expect a good deal of horse trading in the next few days as coalition partners jostle for power and try to agree on who would be best suited for Thailand's top job after the three-day censure debate.
A new prime minister is not expected to be announced until later in the week, government sources said.
Banharn survived the no-confidence vote 207-180 after making a deal with his coalition partners to step down in exchange for their support in the vote.
Several coalition partners, led by the second-largest New Aspiration Party (NAP), threatened to withdraw their support for Banharn in the no-confidence vote if he did not vow to resign.
Now power struggles would begin within the coalition as Chart Thai and NAP were expected to propose candidates for the premiership.

NAP leader, Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, was seen as front runner for the post. Chavalit, 64, who has made no secret of his desire to be prime minister, on Sunday refused to comment on rumours he might be Banharn's successor.
But the Chart Thai party, which has 91 seats in the coalition to NAP's 57, was also expected to present a candidate.
Political analysts and politicians said although Banharn was basically forced to resign, the Chart Thai still held a trump card in Banharn's one week grace period.

"He's buying time," Somjai said. "The NAP will be forced to negotiate with Chart Thai because if they can't reach a deal Chart Thai could threaten to go to an opposition party to form a new government."

A dissolution of the house still could not be ruled out, analysts and politicians said, even though the agreement made between Banharn and his coalition partners was seen as a way to avoid such a step.
Chumpol Silpa-archa, Banharn's younger brother and a Chart Thai member of parliament, said the prime minister still had the authority to dissolve parliament.

"If there is a quarrel over who should become the next prime minister, if each party is pushing for its leader to take the top job and no agreement can be reached, the prime minister may consider dissolving the House," he told reporters.
Most analysts expect a new prime minister will be chosen from the coalition, follwed by a massive reshuffle of the cabinet in order to restore credibility.
"There is no confidence in this government. A new government will have the same problems," one political analyst said.
Banharn was accused in the no-confidence debate of condoning corruption in his government and mismanaging the economy during his 14 months in office.
The stock market sank near to three-year lows, the baht was clouded by repeated devaluation rumours and the economy and exports slowed during Banharn's tenure.
Analysts said if the coalition fails to instill confidence with its new line-up, it may be forced to call fresh elections.
